task.description:
RE-GATE PROVENANCE: This is the re-gate of TEST-DESIGNER's rework 1 (step-04-test-designer-rework1.json), following this validator's own prior FAIL (step-04b-test-design-validator.json).

WF-03 Step 4b re-gate (rework 1 of 3) for ISS-0446. TEST-DESIGNER accepted the prior FAIL, independently reproduced the counterexample, and committed one new deterministic (trap_exit-based) regression-guard test plus a corrected test/specs/ISS-0446.md. Re-verify adversarially: (1) reliability under real load/contention, not just isolation; (2) soundness of the trap_exit choice; (3) whether the guard actually catches reintroduction of check-then-act AT THE REAL FIX SITE, not merely mutation of itself; (4) honesty of the synthetic-child framing; (5) whether the spec's REVISION NOTE corrects rather than drops the prior false claim; (6) runtime cost.

result.summary:
VERDICT: FAIL. Items 1, 2, 5, 6 pass cleanly. Item 3 -- the one that matters most, since it is the entire point of committing this test -- does not: the guard does not reliably catch a reintroduction of the check-then-act pattern at the actual fix site (the neighboring test, lines 1113-1134). It only reliably discriminates a mutation of ITSELF.

=== ITEM 1: RELIABILITY UNDER LOAD -- PASS, strong evidence ===
Ran the new test far beyond TEST-DESIGNER's own 5+5 sample:
- Isolated (mix test ..._test.exs --only line:1136), 15 runs with distinct seeds 1-15: 'Result: 1 passed, 42 excluded' every single time. 15/15 clean.
- Whole modified file (its own internal test suite provides real concurrency/DB contention), 8 runs with distinct seeds: 'Result: 43 passed' every time. 8/8 clean.
- Full suite, once, under GENUINE maximal real-world contention (all 3187 tests + 6 properties, real async:true parallelism across the whole tree, real Postgres load) -- the single strongest test for flakiness available in this environment. Ran it as a blocking foreground call (per this project's 'No Background Wait For A Cross-Turn Notification' rule -- when the tool auto-backgrounded it past its own timeout window, I polled synchronously for the process's own completion rather than treating any cross-turn notification as my resumption signal). REAL QUOTED OUTPUT: 'Finished in 1445.9 seconds (21.8s async, 1424.0s sync)', 'Result: 3193 passed (6 properties, 3187 tests), 21 excluded'. Zero failures, and no failure output naming the new test (ExUnit only prints names on failure, consistent with a clean pass folded into the 3193). Total: 24 independent clean observations across three escalating levels of real contention, zero flakiness found. This comfortably clears the 'would a new flaky test be actively harmful' bar TEST-DESIGNER was held to.

=== ITEM 2: TRAP_EXIT SOUNDNESS -- PASS ===
TEST-DESIGNER's reasoning holds under my own scrutiny: trap_exit converts the child's own death from 'sometimes fast, sometimes slow depending on unrelated BEAM scheduling' into 'always exactly as slow as terminate/2's own sleep,' which removes a second, unrelated noise source rather than substituting a different mechanism for the one this issue is about. The race being guarded (the on_exit-runner process's Process.alive?/1 check racing the link-exit signal reaching the supervisor) is structurally the same with or without trap_exit -- trap_exit only makes the window's WIDTH deterministic, not its EXISTENCE. I did not find a way this could be testing something adjacent instead: the stacktrace produced under mutation (see Item 3 below) is byte-identical in shape to the original CI failure and to the non-trapping async:true/async:false reproductions from the prior round.

=== ITEM 3: DOES THE GUARD ACTUALLY GUARD THE STATED PROPERTY -- FAIL, the decisive finding ===
ORCH's own verification mutated the GUARD TEST ITSELF to the old shape and got 0/1 passed on 3/3 runs -- confirming the guard discriminates mutation of itself. I tested the scenario the guard's own comment names as its purpose: 'nobody can reintroduce a check-then-act on_exit guard on top of it later.' The real fix site for that scenario is the NEIGHBORING test (lines 1113-1134, the one ISS-0446 originally patched) -- NOT the guard test. I reintroduced the exact deleted pattern there (Supervisor.start_link/2, unnamed, name: __MODULE__.MutatedThrowawaySupervisor + on_exit(fn -> if Process.alive?(sup_pid), do: Supervisor.stop(sup_pid) end)), leaving the new guard test at line ~1136 completely untouched, and ran the full file repeatedly:
  - 5 seeded runs (seeds 1-5): 4/5 clean ('43 passed'), 1/5 caught it ('42/43 passed', seed 3).
  - Re-ran seed 3 alone in isolation afterward: passed clean ('43 passed') -- confirming the catch was itself non-deterministic (real DB/scheduler timing on the day, not a repeatable seed-driven failure).
  - 10 further unseeded runs: 9/10 clean, 1/10 caught it (run 4).
  TOTAL: 2/15 (~13%) of runs caught the reintroduced bug -- and NOT via the new guard test, which passed every single time in all 15 runs (it does not touch the mutated code at all, since it uses its own separate SlowTrapChild fixture). The 2 catches came from the ORIGINAL probabilistic mechanism resurfacing directly in the unwidened, mutated fix-site test itself -- the same intermittent on_exit crash ISS-0446 was filed over in the first place, at roughly the same order-of-magnitude rate CI originally saw it (ISS-0446.yaml: 1/3192 on the reporting CI run).
  Reverted the mutation with `git checkout -- test/letflow/engine/service_task_dispatcher_test.exs`; verified: `git status --porcelain test/ lib/` empty, SHA256 of the restored file (`e34091b81d3eddf01b11553eeee7574a0a464c47fa5a6e15391347c2da3fc3f4`) matches the pristine pre-mutation hash exactly, and a fresh run post-revert: `mix test test/letflow/engine/service_task_dispatcher_test.exs` -> `Result: 43 passed`.
  CONSEQUENCE: the guard's own stated purpose -- protecting against someone reintroducing this exact pattern 'on top of it later' -- is NOT delivered for the realistic version of that event (an edit at the fix site itself, the guard left alone). The guard is airtight against a mutation of ITS OWN 8 lines, and essentially inert (no better than the pre-fix status quo) against a regression at the actual site it exists to protect. This is precisely the gap between 'catches mutation of itself' and 'catches the regression it claims to guard' that Item 3's dispatch asked me to check for by name, and it is real.

=== ITEM 4: SYNTHETIC-CHILD FRAMING -- PASS ===
Unchanged from the sound argument already accepted: the real Poller neither traps exits nor does slow terminate/2 work, so it would not exercise the teardown window regardless of fixture idiom. A synthetic child is a structural necessity for testing timing behavior the real child does not have, not evasion of the 'this tests ExUnit, not Letflow' concern -- the property under test (this suite's chosen idiom's teardown behavior under load) is still a Letflow-suite-owned choice, even though the vehicle exercising it is synthetic. My Item 3 finding does not change this judgment; the synthetic-child choice itself is fine, the problem is what the resulting test does and does not detect.

=== ITEM 5: SPEC HONESTY -- PASS ===
The REVISION NOTE section explicitly states the original claim was 'WRONG' and 'RETRACTED', names the specific false claim, cites the validator's counterexample, and states what survives (async:true numbers, 8-file finding, caveat framing) versus what was replaced. This is a correction, not a silent drop -- matches the standard the initial dispatch and this project's norms require.

=== ITEM 6: RUNTIME COST -- PASS, negligible ===
The new test alone runs in ~0.4-0.5s per TEST-DESIGNER's own isolated measurement (consistent with my own observation of the isolated-run timings, which were dominated by fixture/DB setup rather than the 5ms sleep itself). Against a 1445.9-second full-suite run, this is immaterial -- roughly 0.03% of total suite time. Not a meaningful cost concern regardless of the Item 3 outcome.

=== CLEANUP ===
All probing was done via a single reverted in-place mutation (no worktree needed for this scale of check) plus scratch/tdv-iss0446-regate/ for log files, both removed. `git status --porcelain` (repo root) returned EMPTY at the end of this gate. No lib/ file was ever touched. The one background-tool auto-timeout event (the full-suite run exceeding the tool's 600s window) was handled by polling for the same foreground process's own completion synchronously, not by treating the resulting cross-turn notification as a resumption signal, per this project's explicit rule against that pattern.

=== WHY THIS IS A FAIL AND NOT A MINOR NOTE ===
The coordinator's own framing was direct: 'If it is genuinely good now, PASS it plainly -- do not manufacture a third round.' I looked for a reason to pass this and could not find one that survives Item 3's result. A regression guard whose entire stated purpose is to prevent a specific reintroduction, but which only reliably catches an attack on its own 8 lines and reverts to the ORIGINAL ~13%-per-run detection rate for the actual reintroduction scenario it names, has not delivered the property TEST-DESIGNER argued for and REVIEWER/coordinator's own mutation check did not test (that check only mutated the guard itself, the same gap I am flagging). This is not 'a well-written argument I'm rubber-stamping' nor 'reflexively demanding more when the case is solid' -- it is a specific, reproduced, reverted-and-verified measurement that contradicts the guard's own justification.

issues.title: The ISS-0446 regression guard test only reliably discriminates mutation of its OWN 8 lines; it does not reliably catch reintroduction of check-then-act at the actual fix site (the neighboring test), reverting to the original ~13%-per-run probabilistic detection for that realistic scenario
issues.description: Reintroduced the exact deleted Supervisor.start_link/2 + on_exit(fn -> if Process.alive?(sup_pid), do: Supervisor.stop(sup_pid) end) pattern into the test at lines 1113-1134 (the real ISS-0446 fix site), leaving the new guard test at line ~1136 (Iss0446RegressionGuard.SlowTrapChild-based) completely untouched. Ran the full file 15 times (5 seeded, 10 unseeded): only 2/15 (~13%) caught the reintroduced bug, and both catches came from the original unwidened race resurfacing directly in the mutated fix-site test itself, not from the new guard (which passed all 15/15 times, since it exercises a separate fixture entirely and never touches the mutated code path). This is roughly the same order-of-magnitude detection rate the original CI flake had (ISS-0446.yaml: 1 failure on the reporting run out of 3192 total tests, i.e. this specific test failing on the order of low tens of percent of the runs where it happens to fire, not 1/3192 overall). ORCH's own mutation verification (referenced in the re-gate dispatch) mutated the guard test itself and correctly found 0/1 passed on 3/3 runs -- but that only demonstrates the guard is a good test OF ITSELF, not that it protects the code its own comment says it protects ('nobody can reintroduce a check-then-act on_exit guard on top of it later'). Reverted via git checkout --, verified SHA256-identical to the pristine pre-mutation file and a clean 43-passed re-run.

result.next_action: Route back to TEST-DESIGNER for rework 2 of 3. Direction, not prescribed as the only path: the guard as committed is a legitimate, reliable, cheap test of the shared fixture idiom in the abstract, and item 1/2/4/5/6 all hold -- it need not be discarded. But it does not by itself satisfy the stated purpose of guarding against reintroduction AT THE FIX SITE. Two non-exclusive options to consider: (a) parametrize/duplicate the guard's SlowTrapChild-based harness to run using the SAME child spec and fixture calls the fix-site test uses (Letflow.Engine.ServiceTaskDispatcher.Poller wrapped or substituted with a trap_exit+slow-terminate variant), so a future check-then-act edit AT the fix site would need to defeat the same widened-window mechanism, not merely coexist beside it; (b) accept the guard's narrower, already-valid scope (protecting the suite's own fixture idiom in the abstract) but correct the test's own comment and test/specs/ISS-0446.md to stop claiming it protects against reintroduction 'on top of it later' at the specific fix site, since measurement shows it does not -- and treat the fix site's own future safety as resting on REVIEWER's structural argument (no Process.alive? in terminate_supervisor/2) plus ordinary code review, not on this test. Either is legitimate; re-derive rather than picking blindly, and report the measurement (my 2/15 figure or your own independent re-measurement, per this project's re-derive-don't-inherit rule) in the resulting spec update.
